title: Dharma talk with Juriki Samuel Senerchia at Samish Sesshin
speaker: Juriki Samuel Senerchia
summary: Juriki Samuel Senerchia's main teaching is that true appreciation and comfort can be found in the present moment, particularly in our physical bodies. By cultivating awareness of our breath and posture, we can let go of tension and anxiety, and find peace and connection to ourselves and the world around us. This practice of being present and aware can be a powerful tool for navigating life's challenges, including those related to mortality and the end of life. By embracing the present moment, we can find comfort and solace in the here and now.

sentences.text: Please forgive me for disturbing your zazen.
I know you all came here to practice zazen.
Thank you for this opportunity, Nomon, inviting me to teach.
Thank you, Alison, for your talk this morning.
It's very enjoyable.
I was just thinking about the talk from this morning, the Platform Sutra.
There was a piece in it that spoke to me, spoke very clearly of our teaching: to be humble, to see all beings as Buddha, and to be of service.
It seemed like it was right there in a different language, but easy to translate.
I really appreciate it, bringing some more wisdom on the topic that I brought up.
So this evening, there's been a request for me to share some more of my poetry, so to speak.
I don't really like to call it poetry.
But I thought I would.
I was thinking about words.
Words are an attempt to share a feeling.
To say something is an art, and it really has nothing to do with the words.
It has to do with the feeling in our heart, trying to communicate.
And so if you are listening with ears to try to gain something, you will miss it.
And if I am trying to say something with the mind of trying to gain something, I will miss it.
But when arrow points meet head on, what has this to do with skill?
So we dive in.
Somehow words work better for me on the [unclear: "ink line of paper"].
So this was from last weekend, sharing a feeling.
*Wide, smooth, clear, deep rolling river.
Giant maple tree dropped her colorful leaves on thick moist green grass.
We walk with happy hearts to be here.
Down the bank into the river bed.
I give my breath and praise.
Touching water, cupping hands bring her to touch my face.
She awakens me.*
*A prayer of gratitude for all these relatives.
An eagle flies upstream.
The rain gently falls.
A prayer asking for help parenting.
Remembering our boys.
Teenagers spreading their wings.
One out there on his own doing his first year away from the nest, making choices, enjoying the freedom of being alone.
Bless him.*
*The other still in the nest, exploring love and social environments.
I remember to return to faith.
It's all good.
At the river's edge, we stand offering sacred ground corn.
I am blessed to be the father of two beautiful children.
And the partner of this beautiful woman right here.
Touching water, I am blessed.
I give thanks.*
*Joy fills my heart as mountains tower above.
Newly covered with snow, icicles decorate cliffs at the pass.
Snow laden trees line this portal to another land.
Descending thousands of feet, evergreen gives way to grasslands.
A different kind of river valley.
Aspen and cottonwood, all yellows and oranges, fill this river bed as it meanders magnificently.
We arrive on the family farm by evening.
Father out tending the horses.*
*Children smile as they play.
Grandmother harvests vegetable gardens for dinner.
Animals gather in for a cold night.
Everywhere this place calls to me, welcome home.
Grassy hills, clear, dark sky full of stars.
Family gathered patiently around an old wooden table.
With mix-matched chairs, it is warm from the baking of dinner.
Everyone is seated at a place appropriate to their role.*
*The single overhead electric light is dimmed.
Homemade candles warmly draw us together intimately.
We take hands and share a minute of silence and stillness.
To give thanks, no words are required.
Eight people are served from a single salmon flank.
As we hear the story of father and children pulling a fish from its migration according to tradition and conditions.
Hand-carved wooden bowls and spoons, hand-blown water glasses.
It is plentiful and beautiful.*
*Homegrown potatoes, vegetables with garlic.
We take turns organically sharing and listening.
Children, elders, parents, we are all nourished, body and soul.
This is a spiritual meal.
It is just enough.
Under the starry sky, a shooting star flashes down the Milky Way.
Stillness holds us all.
Long before the sun, a quarter moon gives light.*
*I am eager to greet this day, this place.
Quietly in the dark, I check in with all the farm animals and wander across fields down to the creek.
Yellow leaves carpet the ground as light returns.
Still pooled, frozen over, cold water touches me deeply.*
So how do we appreciate our life?
How do we appreciate the natural world that we live in that gives us life?
How do we appreciate family and friends growing together?
As we did memorial service this evening for Laura, it was touched by the truth that one grief touches all grief.
As Nomon offered words of love and remembrance, in my heart I felt the passing a few months ago of my mother-in-law, of my cousin a few months before that.
And I may not have talked about this, but I work as a palliative care chaplain.
So I work with dying people all the time.
Sometimes three a week, sometimes more, less.
It's pretty scary to face your death with disease-wracked body.
And so I just try to accompany people and offer some comfort, some assurance that their life matters.
Some friendship to listen, try to find out what brings them hope and happiness.
So one more poem from a few days later.
*I am grateful for family and friends.
Grateful for farmers producing food by labor and knowledge.
Intimate with land.
Grateful for fresh water.
Everything in the world has a nature, a story, a origin, a lover, and a mother.
My mother is the fresh water in everything.
I hear her voice splashing over rocks.*
*She is everywhere I go.
I go to her with joy.
Learn awareness inward.
Examine the subtle movements of this heart.
Learn the origins of behaviors.
What causes me to get scared and lose faith?
Old wounds, old stories.
Learn the stories.*
*Find the riddle and keep turning it slowly.
Sing on every side till the smell of truth fills your mind.
Till you taste the irony of being the only one that can give away the very gift you always longed for.
It is the longing that is the gift.
Longing is prayer.
Prayer is not an old story, but the lover's longing for comfort.
To belong is to follow your story all the way back to its origin.
To Mother Nature.*
*Restless wandering comes to sit without refusing anything.*
I really like that one.
I like that piece about longing is the gift.
So the title of my class was actually Embodied Zen and the Twelve Step Recovery.
And in one of my classes, maybe more than one class, I talked a little bit about the three information processing centers in the body.
You might call these mind.
There's the verbal mind located in the neurons of the brain.
And there's the feeling mind located in the neurons of the heart, lungs.
And there's the feeling, or what do you call it, instinctual intelligence, neurons located in the gut.
And I think one of our Sunday classes, or maybe one of our Wednesday evenings, I directed some attention to these three different locations.
And I thought it would be worth returning to now.
So if you don't mind, if you would care to join me, bring your attention to your posture, starting with your contact with earth, which might be your knees or feet, maybe your sit bones.
And just really bring your attention deeply into that contact.
Feel the weight, touch.
Dogen's instructions remind us to rock the body back and forth a little bit.
Norman's teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman, always reminded us: if you think you know that you're in upright posture, you've missed it.
He said, keep looking for it.
It's not a place that is holding still.
It's a place to be curious about.
So feel that contact below the spine and see if you can bring your awareness into the first vertebrae.
Some of you have space between your vertebrae, bottom of your spine.
There's muscles that pull the body into this upright position deep inside the pelvic.
Edward Brown, one of my early teachers, talked about how important it was to let the belly extend forward and be soft.
So maybe you can exaggerate that a little bit.
Deep breath and then just let that out and relax.
Maintain that shape.
A question that I always sit with is, what is the shape of my spine?
Actually feel the shape.
Stack each bone on top of the next.
What is there?
Is there tension, pain, anxiety, grief, anger, fear?
Breathe into it.
Fill it with your breath.
Pull the belly and, traveling up to the chest and the thoracic spine, it's helpful to pick up the shoulders and pull them back and down.
See if you can make a little bit more space for your heart.
Up, back, down, maybe up and then just drop.
If you can find tension, let it go.
Pull the elbows away from the body.
The instruction is to feel that there could be an egg under your armpit.
It's open, it's not clenched.
So this is the heart center, the place where we connect.
Bring in, give out, bring some awareness into your heart.
How does the diaphragm feel?
Is there tension there?
Maybe your heart hurts, maybe your shoulders hurt.
Just be gentle with yourself.
Coming into the cervical spine.
Neck is long.
The instruction is as if you were being picked up by one hair, or one golden thread, into the heavens.
Let that lift you up gently.
There's 28 muscles throughout your head.
Try to relax them.
See if you can find them.
I assume there's half on each side, so that's only 14.
Left and right.
How's your forehead?
Eyebrows?
Around your eyes.
Your eyeballs themselves.
Your ears, cheeks, nostrils, lips, jaw.
Breathe in and relax.
Check back in.
What has gotten tight by now?
So in the practice of zazen, I talked about last week, I think, the practice of self-inquiry.
Who is this?
Norman was talking about that yesterday.
Huatou.
Who is this?
Let's take a minute together to just check in.
Zazen is not about anybody telling you anything.
It's just settling.
I don't know if you all have noticed, but on the wall up here there's a giant cross.
It's a beautiful symbol for the human being.
We have this great conduit between earth and heaven: our spinal cord.
So I'm going to invite you now to envision this spinal cord, this energy conduit, and send roots down into the earth.
With each exhale, relax further down into the earth.
Inhale and let the energy come up the spine.
Leave the top of the head.
I know that's why we don't wear hats in the center.
Let the energy out the top of the head.
Exhaling, relaxing deep into the roots of the body.
Solid ground.
Inhale all the way to heaven.
Boundless body of Buddha.
This cross has arms just like us.
Come into your heart center.
To your awareness.
To your breath.
Open up. [unclear: "Mou jiao"].
Calm and settling.
Shikantaza includes both of these.
I think I said the other week that shikantaza itself was not adequate.
I may have misspoken.
I was thinking about that more.
For me, I think shikantaza includes both self-inquiry and calming, concentration practice.
So feel yourself as this holy cross you've been sitting under the last couple days.
Planted deeply in the earth.
Reaching up.
Two arms.
Embracing all beings.
I'd like to invite anybody who would like to shout out some words right now.
What is this?
What do you find?
I'd like to continue this investigation of embodied presence in walking.
So we're going to close lecture form and return to our seats.
And we're going to begin kinhin.
Unless it would do you bodily harm, I would invite you to stay in the zendo.
And I will offer some kinhin instruction.
Thank you for your devoted attention.
